claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to gene association studies.

claims.claim: Gpr88 gene transcript levels were found modified following exposure to mood stabilizers.
claims.source: In rodents, transcript levels of Gpr88 gene were found modified following exposure to various psychoactive drugs, such as mood stabilizers, antidepressants, methamphetamine, L-DOPA and drugs of abuse (Conti et al., 2007; Ogden et al., 2004; Brandish et al., 2005; Le Merrer et al., 2012; Becker et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Deletion of the Gpr88 gene in mice alters primarily striatal physiology.
claims.source: In mice, deletion of the Gpr88 gene alters primarily striatal physiology, striatum-centered brain networks and striatal-dependent behaviors, with notably severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning, hyperactivity, stereotypies and altered reward-driven behaviors (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Meirsman et al., 2016b; Rainwater et al., 2017; Ben Hamida et al., 2018; Arefin et al., 2017; Quintana et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Deletion of the Gpr88 gene in mice causes severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning.
claims.source: In mice, deletion of the Gpr88 gene alters primarily striatal physiology, striatum-centered brain networks and striatal-dependent behaviors, with notably severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning, hyperactivity, stereotypies and altered reward-driven behaviors (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Meirsman et al., 2016b; Rainwater et al., 2017; Ben Hamida et al., 2018; Arefin et al., 2017; Quintana et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Deletion of the Gpr88 gene in mice causes hyperactivity.
claims.source: In mice, deletion of the Gpr88 gene alters primarily striatal physiology, striatum-centered brain networks and striatal-dependent behaviors, with notably severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning, hyperactivity, stereotypies and altered reward-driven behaviors (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Meirsman et al., 2016b; Rainwater et al., 2017; Ben Hamida et al., 2018; Arefin et al., 2017; Quintana et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: GPR88 is considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs.
claims.source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classification studies.

claims.claim: GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of the class A GPCR family.
claims.source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classification studies.

claims.claim: GPR88 displays an unusually short C-terminus of 14 amino acids.
claims.source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
claims.evidence: This is a structural characteristic of GPR88 based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: GPR88 displays a large non-homologous third intracellular loop of 67 amino acids.
claims.source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
claims.evidence: This is a structural characteristic of GPR88 based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Based on the sequence of its putative transmembrane binding pocket, GPR88 clusters with class C GPCRs.
claims.source: Moreover, based on the sequence of its putative transmembrane binding pocket, GPR88 clusters with class C GPCRs, for which the endogenous ligands bind in the large N-terminus domain (Surgand et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a classification study.

claims.claim: Intensive efforts in deorphanizing GPR88 have remained vain.
claims.source: Intensive efforts in deorphanizing GPR88 have remained vain (Bi et al., 2015; Decker et al., 2017; Dzierba et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2014); meanwhile, synthetic chemistry met significant difficulties in identifying potent agonists for this atypical receptor (Bi et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple deorphanization attempts.

claims.claim: GPR88 was shown to display constitutive and ligand-induced activity on Gαi/o/z inhibitory protein coupling in heterologous and native cells.
claims.source: Although this receptor was shown to display constitutive and ligand-induced activity on Gαi/o/z inhibitory protein coupling in heterologous and native cells (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Dzierba et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2018), its ability to recruit β-arrestins and intracellular trafficking have not been investigated yet.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The ability of GPR88 to recruit β-arrestins and intracellular trafficking have not been investigated prior to this study.
claims.source: Although this receptor was shown to display constitutive and ligand-induced activity on Gαi/o/z inhibitory protein coupling in heterologous and native cells (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Dzierba et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2018), its ability to recruit β-arrestins and intracellular trafficking have not been investigated yet.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's investigations.

claims.claim: Orphan GPCRs may influence the signaling of other GPCRs in a ligand-independent manner through hetero-oligomerization, as shown for GPR50.
claims.source: Interestingly, it was proposed that orphan GPCRs may influence the signaling of other GPCRs in a ligand-independent manner through hetero-oligomerization, as shown for GPR50 (Levoye et al., 2006a; Levoye et al., 2006b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on GPR50.

claims.claim: There was an increase in [35S]-GTPγS binding of striatal membranes from Gpr88-/- mice in response to stimulation by agonists of the muscarinic and opioid delta (δOR) and mu (μOR) receptors.
claims.source: Remarkably, we have evidenced in a previous study (Meirsman et al., 2016a) an increase in [35S]-GTPγS binding of striatal membranes from Gpr88-/- mice in response to stimulation by agonists of the muscarinic and opioid delta (δOR) and mu (μOR) receptors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claims.claim: Behavioral features of Gpr88-/- mice intriguingly oppose several aspects of the phenotype of mice lacking δOR (Oprd1-/-).
claims.source: Moreover, we noticed that behavioral features of these mutants intriguingly oppose several aspects of the phenotype of mice lacking δOR (Oprd1-/-) and that pharmacological blockade of δOR ameliorate behavioral deficits in Gpr88 knockout mice.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from previous work comparing phenotypes.

claims.claim: Pharmacological blockade of δOR ameliorates behavioral deficits in Gpr88 knockout mice.
claims.source: Moreover, we noticed that behavioral features of these mutants intriguingly oppose several aspects of the phenotype of mice lacking δOR (Oprd1-/-) and that pharmacological blockade of δOR ameliorate behavioral deficits in Gpr88 knockout mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from previous work.

claims.claim: GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with δOR, indicating close physical proximity.
claims.source: We evidenced that GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with the three opioid receptors, δOR, κOR and µOR, indicative of close physical proximity (within 10 nm) to them, in addition to itself (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with κOR, indicating close physical proximity.
claims.source: We evidenced that GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with the three opioid receptors, δOR, κOR and µOR, indicative of close physical proximity (within 10 nm) to them, in addition to itself (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with µOR, indicating close physical proximity.
claims.source: We evidenced that GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with the three opioid receptors, δOR, κOR and µOR, indicative of close physical proximity (within 10 nm) to them, in addition to itself (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: GPR88 possibly forms hetero-oligomers with all opioid receptors.
claims.source: These results indicate that GPR88 possibly forms hetero-oligomers with all opioid receptors.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the BRET data showing close proximity.

claims.claim: Growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced δOR inhibition of cAMP accumulation.
claims.source: While δOR cell surface expression (measured using anti-HA antibody, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) remained constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced δOR inhibition of cAMP accumulation (Gαi/o-dependent pathway) and β-arrestin2 (β−arr2) recruitment (and similarly β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claims.claim: Growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced β-arrestin2 recruitment at δOR.
claims.source: While δOR cell surface expression (measured using anti-HA antibody, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) remained constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced δOR inhibition of cAMP accumulation (Gαi/o-dependent pathway) and β-arrestin2 (β−arr2) recruitment (and similarly β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claims.claim: GPR88 expression interfered with δOR/β−arr2 interactions under stimulated conditions only.
claims.source: We evidenced that the probability of β−arr2 recruitment at δOR was low under basal conditions and high when δOR was stimulated. GPR88 expression interfered with δOR/β−arr2 interactions under stimulated conditions only.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET experiments measuring β-arrestin recruitment under different conditions.

claims.claim: Co-expressing GPR88 with δOR is sufficient to affect G protein and β-arrestin dependent signaling pathways and trafficking of δOR.
claims.source: Altogether, these data indicate that co-expressing GPR88 with δOR is sufficient to affect G protein and β-arrestin dependent signaling pathways and trafficking of the latter.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: GPR88 expression decreased U50488H-activated κOR pathway to Gαi/o, although to a lesser extent than for δOR.
claims.source: GPR88 expression decreased U50488H-activated κOR pathway to Gαi/o, although in our hands to a lesser extent than for δOR (decrease up to 27.7% of maximal effect versus 61.1% for δOR) and only for the highest dose of GPR88 cDNA, without altering κOR cell surface expression Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative dose-response experiments.

claims.claim: GPR88 had a significant inhibitory effect on agonist-induced β−arr2 recruitment at κOR.
claims.source: GPR88, however, had a significant inhibitory effect on agonist-induced β−arr2 recruitment at κOR (and β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by β-arrestin recruitment experiments.

claims.claim: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-activated Gαi/o pathway of µOR.
claims.source: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-activated Gαi/o pathway and β−arr2 recruitment of µOR (see also β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), µOR expression remaining stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claims.claim: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-induced β−arr2 recruitment of µOR.
claims.source: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-activated Gαi/o pathway and β−arr2 recruitment of µOR (see also β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), µOR expression remaining stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claims.claim: Expressing GPR88 reduced the affinity of β−arr2 for DAMGO-stimulated µOR to that measured under basal conditions.
claims.source: Focusing on β−arr2/µOR interactions, we observed again that β−arr2 had significantly more affinity for µOR under stimulated versus basal conditions. Expressing GPR88 reduced the affinity of β−arr2 for DAMGO-stimulated µOR to that measured under basal conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET experiments measuring β-arrestin affinity.

claims.claim: DAMGO-induced µOR stimulation produced an increase in the phospho-ERK/total ERK ratio that was suppressed in the presence of GPR88.
claims.source: We verified that DAMGO-induced µOR stimulation produced an increase in the phospho-ERK/total ERK total (pERK/tERK) ratio that was suppressed in the presence of GPR88 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Pertussis toxin markedly reduced the early phase of DAMGO-induced phosphorylation of ERK, showing its dependence on G protein recruitment (Gi/o).
claims.source: Addition of pertussis toxin (PTX) markedly reduced the early phase of DAMGO-induced phosphorylation of ERK, showing its dependence on G protein recruitment (Gi/o).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PTX treatment experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: GPR88 expression completely blocked DAMGO-induced phosphorylation of ERK.
claims.source: PTX, however, failed to suppress a later phase of DAMGO-induced response, while GPR88 expression did (Figure 2B) (see gels in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of GPR88 on µOR signaling weakens when µOR amounts increase, with a complete restoration for high doses of µOR.
claims.source: We showed that the inhibitory effect of GPR88 on µOR signaling weakens when µOR amounts increase, with a complete restoration for high doses of µOR (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Increasing the amount of µOR was not able to completely overcome the inhibitory effect of GPR88 on β-arr2 recruitment at µOR.
claims.source: In contrast, increasing the amount of µOR was not able to completely overcome the inhibitory effect of GPR88 (30 ng of cDNA) on β-arr2 recruitment at µOR; notably, no further recruitment was observed over 50 ng of µOR cDNA transfected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: GPR88 inhibitory action on G-protein dependent µOR signaling was more sensitive to µOR level of expression than its blunting effects on β-arrestin recruitment.
claims.source: In conclusion, GPR88 inhibitory action on G-protein dependent µOR signaling was more sensitive to µOR level of expression than its blunting effects on β-arrestin recruitment, suggesting different mechanisms of interaction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of varying µOR expression on different signaling pathways.

claims.claim: Morphine injections induced a significant rise in locomotor activity that progressively sensitized upon repeated administration in both Gpr88-/- and Gpr88+/+ mice.
claims.source: In both mouse lines, morphine injections induced a significant rise in locomotor activity that progressively sensitized upon repeated administration (Figure 3A, panel a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Locomotor activation and sensitization were markedly exacerbated in Gpr88-/- compared to Gpr88+/+ mice.
claims.source: Locomotor activation and sensitization, however, were markedly exacerbated in Gpr88-/- compared to Gpr88+/+ mice (panel b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Gpr88 deletion facilitates morphine-induced locomotion and sensitization.
claims.source: These results thus indicate that Gpr88 deletion facilitates morphine-induced locomotion and sensitization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the locomotor activity experiments.

claims.claim: Gpr88-/- mice lost more body weight than controls upon exposure to escalating doses of morphine.
claims.source: Upon exposure to escalating doses of morphine (n = 6 per treatment and genotype), Gpr88-/- lost more body weight than controls (panel a; Treatment: F1,20=43.7, p=0.0000; Day: F4,80=13.6, p=0.0000; Day x Genotype: F4,80=5.1, p=0.001; Day x Treatment: F4,80=9.9, p=0.0000; body weight was measured daily upon morphine treatment)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: When withdrawal was triggered by acute naloxone administration, Gpr88-/- animals displayed sniffing episodes quicker than their Gpr88+/+ counterparts.
claims.source: when withdrawal was triggered by acute naloxone administration (1 mg/kg), mutant animals displayed sniffing episodes (panel b; Genotype/Treatment: F1,20=25.5, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,20=23.1, p=0.0001; Time: F3,60=10.5, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype/Treatment: F3,60=9.3, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype x Treatment: F3,60=8.3, p=0.0001) and vegetative signs of withdrawal (panel c; Genotype: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Treatment: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Time: F3,60=14.4, p=0.0000) quicker than their Gpr88+/+ counterparts
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by withdrawal experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Gpr88-/- and Gpr88+/+ mice displayed similar final withdrawal scores.
claims.source: when withdrawal was triggered by acute naloxone administration (1 mg/kg), mutant animals displayed sniffing episodes (panel b; Genotype/Treatment: F1,20=25.5, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,20=23.1, p=0.0001; Time: F3,60=10.5, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype/Treatment: F3,60=9.3, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype x Treatment: F3,60=8.3, p=0.0001) and vegetative signs of withdrawal (panel c; Genotype: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Treatment: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Time: F3,60=14.4, p=0.0000) quicker than their Gpr88+/+ counterparts, despite similar final withdrawal scores (panel d; Treatment: F1,20=38.9, p=0.0000)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by withdrawal experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Gpr88-/- mice acquired preference for a compartment associated to morphine administration similarly as Gpr88+/+ animals.
claims.source: Gpr88-/-mice acquired preference for a compartment associated to morphine administration (10 mg/Kg) similarly as Gpr88+/+ animals (panel a; Treatment: F1,28=45.8, p=0.0000; Conditioning: F1,28=15.7, p=0.0005; Conditioning x Treatment: F1,28=31.1, p=0.0000)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by CPP experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Gpr88-/- mice extinguished morphine place preference conditioning quicker than wild-type counterparts.
claims.source: they extinguished this conditioning quicker than wild-type counterparts (panel b; Genotype: F1,28=10.3, p=0034; Treatment: F1,28=6.5, p=0166; Genotype x Treatment: F1,28=5.0, p=0329; Session: F9,252=5.2, p=0.0000; Session x Treatment: F9,252=3.7, p=0.0002)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by CPP extinction experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Gpr88-/- and Gpr88+/+ mice reinstated morphine place preference at comparable levels.
claims.source: and finally reinstated morphine place preference at comparable levels as the latter (panel c; Treatment: F1,28=9.2, p=0.0052)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by CPP reinstatement experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Gpr88-/- mice were significantly less sensitive to morphine analgesia at 48°C and 52°C in the tail flick test.
claims.source: In the tail flick test (n = 7–9 per treatment and genotype), Gpr88-/- mice were significantly less sensitive to morphine analgesia at 48°C and 52°C (Genotype: F1,83=22.0, p=0.0000; Treatment: F1,83=84.9, p=0.0000; Temperature: F2,83=162.5, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,83=15.9, p=0.0001; Treatment x Temperature: F2,83=5.4, p=0.0065)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by tail immersion test experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In the hot plate test, morphine-induced analgesia measured by increased jumping latency was increased in Gpr88 null mice versus controls.
claims.source: in the hot plate test (n = 15–16 per treatment and genotype), morphine-induced analgesia was detected by increased jumping latency in treated animals (right panel); this effect was increased in Gpr88 null mice versus controls (Treatment: F1,59=79.7, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,59=4.0, p=0.0490)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hot plate test experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Pharmacological activation of GPR88 by Compound 19 drastically reduced morphine-induced locomotor activity but left the amplitude of sensitization unchanged.
claims.source: Exposure to morphine (IP, 10 mg/kg) induced an increase in locomotor activity that sensitized upon repeated administration in both vehicle and Compound 19-treated groups (panel a); pharmacological activation of GPR88 drastically reduced morphine-induced locomotor activity but left the amplitude of sensitization unchanged (Morphine effect: F1,30=305.1, p=0.0000; Compound 19: F1,30=55.3, p=0.0000; Day: F2,60=33.1, p=0.0000; Day x Morphine: F2,60=31.6, p=0.0000; Day x Morphine x Compound 19: F2,60=2.1, NS)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity experiments with Compound 19 shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: GPR88 displayed saturated BRET signals with all tested striatal GPCRs except the dopamine D1 receptor.
claims.source: Remarkably, GPR88 displayed saturated BRET signals with all tested striatal GPCRs except the dopamine D1 receptor (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: BRET signal between GPR88 and V2R was unsaturated.
claims.source: In contrast, BRET signal was unsaturated for interactions with the two GPCRs identified as not expressed in CNS neurons, V2R and CXCR4 receptors (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: BRET signal between GPR88 and CXCR4 was unsaturated.
claims.source: In contrast, BRET signal was unsaturated for interactions with the two GPCRs identified as not expressed in CNS neurons, V2R and CXCR4 receptors (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: GPR88 appears to possibly form hetero-oligomers with multiple GPCRs in addition to opioid receptors, notably those GPCRs whose expression is enriched in striatal regions.
claims.source: Thus GPR88 appears to possibly form hetero-oligomers with multiple GPCRs in addition to opioid receptors, notably those GPCRs whose expression is enriched in striatal regions, where GPR88 is also the most expressed.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from BRET experiments and knowledge of expression patterns.

claims.claim: Increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of dopamine D2 receptor.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of muscarinic M1 receptor.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of muscarinic M4 receptor.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: GPR88 co-expression did not interfere with the G protein mediated signaling of adenosine A2A receptor.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Co-expressing GPR88 with dopamine D1 receptor had no significant effect on D1 G protein dependent signaling, or even increased this signaling.
claims.source: In contrast, co-expressing GPR88 with receptors for which we failed to evidence proximity to it, namely dopamine D1, vasopressin V2R and chemokine CXCR4 receptors, had no significant effect on their G protein dependent signaling, or even increased this signaling (D1 receptor) (Figure 5A, panels b,g,h).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: GPR88 expression markedly blunted CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment under both basal and stimulated conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, GPR88 expression markedly blunted CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment under both basal and stimulated conditions (Figure 5B, panel h).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by β-arrestin recruitment assays shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: GPR88 co-expression inhibits G protein dependent signaling of most GPCRs from which it comes close, and only these.
claims.source: GPR88 co-expression was able to inhibit G protein dependent signaling of most GPCRs from which it comes close, and only these.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on functional assays across multiple GPCRs.

claims.claim: GPR88 co-expression resulted in blunted β-arrestin recruitment by all GPCRs tested.
claims.source: In contrast, such co-expression resulted in blunted β-arrestin recruitment by all GPCRs tested.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on β-arrestin recruitment assays across multiple GPCRs.

claims.claim: CXCR4 co-expression had no deleterious effect on DAMGO-induced µOR signaling on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways.
claims.source: Consistent with no detected proximity, CXCR4 co-expression had no deleterious effect on DAMGO-induced µOR signaling, and conversely µOR co-expression did not modify SDF1-mediated CXCR4 signaling, on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: µOR co-expression did not modify SDF1-mediated CXCR4 signaling on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways.
claims.source: Consistent with no detected proximity, CXCR4 co-expression had no deleterious effect on DAMGO-induced µOR signaling, and conversely µOR co-expression did not modify SDF1-mediated CXCR4 signaling, on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: κOR expression repressed agonist-mediated G protein activation and β-arr2 recruitment by µOR, with which it forms hetero-oligomers.
claims.source: In contrast, κOR expression repressed agonist-mediated G protein activation and β-arr2 recruitment by µOR, with which it forms hetero-oligomers (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: κOR expression had no significant impact on G protein-mediated signaling by CXCR4 but significantly inhibited β-arr2-dependent recruitment by this receptor.
claims.source: Such expression however had no significant impact on G protein-mediated signaling by CXCR4 but significantly inhibited β-arr2-dependent recruitment by this receptor (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: GPR88 had a more significant inhibitory impact on G protein dependent µOR signaling than κOR.
claims.source: Compared to κOR, GPR88 had a more significant inhibitory impact on G protein dependent µOR signaling but similarly blunted µOR-dependent β-arr2 recruitment (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative functional assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: GPR88 was able to repress CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment more than κOR, despite no detectable physical proximity to CXCR4.
claims.source: Finally, although GPR88 had little influence on SDF1-induced G protein activation by CXCR4 (see also Figure 5G), it was able to repress CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment more than κOR, despite no detectable physical proximity to CXCR4 (Figures 4B and 6B).

results.result: GPR88 forms hetero-oligomers with all three opioid receptors (δOR, κOR, and µOR) as demonstrated by saturated BRET signals indicating close physical proximity within 10 nm.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A. The saturated BRET signals provide strong evidence for close physical proximity, which is interpreted as potential hetero-oligomerization. The methodology is appropriate for detecting protein-protein interactions.

results.result: GPR88 co-expression inhibits both G protein-dependent signaling and β-arrestin recruitment at all three opioid receptors (δOR, κOR, µOR) in a dose-dependent manner, with µOR being most severely affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C41 are supported by comprehensive dose-response experiments measuring cAMP inhibition, β-arrestin recruitment, and receptor trafficking shown in Figures 1B-E and supplementary figures. The data consistently demonstrate GPR88's inhibitory effects across multiple signaling pathways and all three opioid receptors.

results.result: GPR88 co-expression completely blocks DAMGO-induced ERK phosphorylation at µOR, including both the early G protein-dependent phase and a later phase that is insensitive to pertussis toxin.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by western blot experiments shown in Figure 2A-B. The use of pertussis toxin to distinguish G protein-dependent from independent signaling is appropriate, and the data clearly show GPR88's complete suppression of ERK phosphorylation.

results.result: The inhibitory effect of GPR88 on µOR G protein-dependent signaling can be overcome by increasing µOR expression, but β-arrestin recruitment remains suppressed, suggesting different mechanisms of interaction for these two pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by dose-response experiments varying µOR expression levels shown in Figure 2C-D. The differential sensitivity to receptor expression levels provides mechanistic insight, though the proposed 1:1 stoichiometry interpretation requires additional validation.

results.result: Gpr88 deletion in mice markedly exacerbates morphine-induced locomotor activation and sensitization compared to wild-type controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by locomotor activity experiments shown in Figure 3A with appropriate statistical analysis (n=5-11 per group, significant genotype × treatment interaction). The behavioral data are consistent with the in vitro findings of GPR88's inhibitory effects on µOR signaling.

results.result: Gpr88-/- mice show facilitated morphine withdrawal symptoms, displaying greater weight loss and earlier onset of withdrawal signs (sniffing and vegetative signs) compared to controls, despite similar final withdrawal scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by withdrawal experiments shown in Figure 3B with appropriate sample sizes (n=6 per group) and statistical analysis. The temporal differences in withdrawal sign appearance are particularly interesting, though the similar final scores suggest complexity in the overall withdrawal response.

results.result: Gpr88-/- mice acquire morphine conditioned place preference (CPP) similarly to wild-type mice, extinguish the conditioning faster, and reinstate preference at comparable levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by CPP experiments shown in Figure 3C with adequate sample sizes (n=8 per group) and appropriate statistical analysis. The differential effects on acquisition versus extinction suggest GPR88's role may be behavior-specific rather than uniformly affecting all µOR-mediated responses.

results.result: Gpr88 deletion has opposing effects on morphine analgesia depending on the test: reduced sensitivity in the tail immersion test (spinal) but increased sensitivity in the hot plate test (supraspinal).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by nociception experiments shown in Figure 3D-E with adequate sample sizes (n=7-16 per group). The opposing effects in different pain tests are intriguing and suggest that GPR88's influence depends on the neural circuits involved, though the mechanistic explanation remains speculative.

results.result: Pharmacological activation of GPR88 by Compound 19 reduces morphine-induced locomotor activity but does not affect the amplitude of sensitization.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by locomotor experiments with Compound 19 shown in Figure 3F (n=8-9 per group). The selective effect on acute locomotor response but not sensitization is consistent with in vitro data suggesting GPR88 activation preferentially affects G protein-dependent signaling over β-arrestin recruitment.

results.result: GPR88 forms hetero-oligomers with multiple striatal GPCRs (D2, A2A, M1, M4, GPR12) but not with D1 receptor or non-neuronal GPCRs (V2R, CXCR4), as demonstrated by saturated versus unsaturated BRET signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4A-B. The selective interaction pattern suggests specificity in GPR88's hetero-oligomerization, which is biologically plausible given the overlapping striatal expression patterns. The methodology is appropriate and consistent with earlier opioid receptor experiments.

results.result: GPR88 co-expression inhibits G protein-dependent signaling of most GPCRs with which it forms hetero-oligomers (D2, M1, M4) but not A2A, and has no effect or increases signaling of receptors without detected proximity (D1, V2R, CXCR4).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 and C72 are supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A. The correlation between physical proximity and functional inhibition strengthens the mechanistic interpretation, though the exception of A2A receptor (proximity without inhibition) indicates that proximity alone is not sufficient for functional effects.

results.result: GPR88 co-expression inhibits β-arrestin recruitment by all GPCRs tested, regardless of whether physical proximity was detected, including both striatal and non-neuronal receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C71, and C73 are supported by β-arrestin recruitment assays shown in Figure 5B. The universal inhibition of β-arrestin recruitment, independent of proximity, is a striking finding that distinguishes this mechanism from the proximity-dependent effects on G protein signaling.

results.result: GPR88 interferes with GPCR signaling both when in close proximity (affecting G protein and β-arrestin pathways) and in the absence of detected proximity (affecting only β-arrestin recruitment), as demonstrated by comparing effects on µOR, κOR, and CXCR4.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 are supported by comparative functional assays shown in Figure 6A-B. The experimental design comparing receptors with and without proximity to GPR88, and including κOR as an additional control, provides strong evidence for two distinct mechanisms of GPR88 action.

results.result: GPR88 displays high basal affinity for β-arrestin2, shows patchy intracellular distribution suggesting vesicular localization, and colocalizes with β-arrestin2 in these compartments with apparent depletion around the brightest GPR88 patches, suggesting β-arrestin sequestration as a mechanism for inhibiting other GPCRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by basal β-arrestin recruitment experiments (Figure 6D) and immunocytochemistry (Figure 6E). The proposed sequestration mechanism is plausible and consistent with the proximity-independent inhibition of β-arrestin recruitment, though the mechanism remains somewhat speculative and would benefit from additional functional validation.

results.result: µOR and κOR closely interact with each other, and CXCR4 forms hetero-oligomers with κOR but not µOR, as demonstrated by BRET experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by BRET experiments shown in Figure 6C. The µOR-κOR interaction confirms previous literature (Fujita et al., 2014), and the selective CXCR4-κOR interaction provides important controls for interpreting the specificity of GPCR hetero-oligomerization.

results.result: GPR88 is a striatal-enriched orphan GPCR with developmental expression changes across species, genetic associations with multiple neuropsychiatric disorders, drug-responsive expression, and knockout mice show striatal-dependent behavioral deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C8-C16 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the biological and clinical relevance of GPR88 but do not represent novel findings from the current study.

results.result: GPR88 is structurally atypical, classified as class A GPCR but distantly related to other class A receptors, with an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids), large third intracellular loop (67 amino acids), and a transmembrane binding pocket that clusters with class C GPCRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 describe structural features of GPR88 supported by citations to classification studies and sequence analysis. These are established characteristics that provide important context for understanding GPR88's atypical pharmacology.

results.result: GPR88 remains an orphan receptor despite intensive deorphanization efforts, displays constitutive and ligand-induced Gαi/o/z coupling, but its β-arrestin recruitment and trafficking had not been investigated prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 establish the state of knowledge about GPR88 pharmacology prior to the current study, supported by appropriate citations. These claims justify the novelty of investigating β-arrestin recruitment and trafficking.

results.result: Prior work showed that orphan GPCRs can influence other GPCR signaling through hetero-oligomerization (GPR50 example), and that Gpr88-/- mice show increased GTPγS binding at muscarinic and opioid receptors, opposing phenotypes to δOR knockout mice, and improvement with δOR blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 summarize prior work from the authors and others that motivated the current study. These are appropriately cited and provide the rationale for investigating GPR88-opioid receptor interactions.
